title: The Five Vowel Signs
short: a, e, i, o and u: five signs that stand for a vowel alone, the first column of the grid.
trouble: Students mix up signs that look alike, such as a and the double-axe-like signs near it. Learn each vowel with its picture-like shape.

blocks.html: Time to learn the signs themselves. In How a Syllabary Works you saw that the first row of the grid holds the vowels alone. These five signs are the most common in Linear B, because Greek words often begin with a vowel or have two vowels side by side.

Five signs stand for a vowel by itself: a, e, i, o and u. They are the first row of the grid, and they write a vowel that has no consonant before it, at the start of a word (a-mi-ni-so) or after another vowel (pa-i-to).

blocks.html: A vowel sign is needed whenever a syllable has no consonant before it. That happens at the start of many words, 𐀀𐀖𐀛𐀰 (Amnisos), 𐀁𐀨 (Hera), 𐀂𐀦 (horse), 𐀃𐀺𐀸 (one-handled), 𐀄 in the middle of 𐀦𐀄𐀒𐀫 (cowherds), and wherever two vowels meet, as in 𐀞𐀂𐀵 (Phaistos).

blocks.name: sc-signs
blocks.cap: e-ra, Hera: the vowel e, then ra. The Greek h is not written, as you will see later.

blocks.html: Why does a syllabary need separate vowel signs at all? Because the other signs always begin with a consonant. A word like Amnisos starts with the sound a, with nothing before it. Without a sign for a alone, the scribe could not begin the word. In the grid, the vowel row is the row whose "consonant" is nothing.

Mixing up signs that look alike. 𐀀 (a) and 𐁀 (a2, read ha) both look like a branching stem; 𐀂 (i) and 𐀩 (re) both have upward prongs. Learn each vowel with its own shape and check the details: a's arms bend down, i has three prongs and a crossbar. The flashcards have a vowel deck for practice.

blocks.title: Read the vowel
blocks.q: What is the first sign of 𐀁𐀨?
steps: It is the tall peak with a box inside.

blocks.title: Which sign?
blocks.q: Which vowel sign stands between pa and to in 𐀞𐀂𐀵 (Phaistos)?
steps: The middle sign has three prongs and a crossbar.
